subject: Astronomy & Space
title: TON 618: The Ultramassive Black Hole
description: A micro-lesson that makes TON 618: The Ultramassive Black Hole usable.

hook.text: TON 618 holds one of the most massive black holes ever found—66 billion times the mass of our Sun.

buildup.text: It powers a quasar so bright it outshines its entire galaxy by a factor of hundreds.

discovery.text: Located 10.4 billion light-years away, its light left when the universe was less than a quarter of its current age.

twist.text: Its event horizon is larger than our entire solar system. Pluto's orbit would fit comfortably inside.

climax.text: How black holes grow this large remains one of astronomy's great puzzles. Mergers alone can't explain it.

punchline.text: Sixty-six billion suns. An event horizon bigger than our solar system.

quiz.question: How massive is the black hole TON 618?

details.summary: TON 618 harbors one of the most massive known black holes — approximately 66 billion solar masses, with an event horizon larger than our entire solar system. This ultraluminous quasar, 10 billion light-years away, shines with the light of 140 trillion Suns, powered by its enormous accretion rate.
details.whyItMatters: TON 618 pushes the known limits of black hole mass and luminosity. Understanding how such extreme objects formed challenges our models of black hole growth and the relationship between black holes and their host galaxies.

faq.question: Is there a maximum size for a black hole?
faq.answer: There may be a practical limit around 50-100 billion solar masses. At extreme masses, radiation from the accretion disk pushes infalling matter away (Eddington limit), slowing growth. However, mergers could bypass this limit. The theoretical maximum remains debated.

faq.question: How is such a distant black hole's mass measured?
faq.answer: Through the width of emission lines in its quasar spectrum. Broader lines indicate faster-moving gas, which implies stronger gravity and greater mass. This 'reverberation mapping' technique relates the size and speed of the emitting gas region to the central black hole's mass.
